sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark.

questions.q: Name the three sub-periods of adulthood.
questions.answer: Young adulthood, middle adulthood and later adulthood (old age).

questions.q: What is the age thirty transition?
questions.answer: Reappraisal in the early thirties of one's career and social relationship choices to make specific changes.

questions.q: State true or false: (i) Body organs decline 0.8–1 per cent per year after age 30. (ii) Sensory abilities change gradually with ageing.
questions.answer: (i) True. (ii) True.

questions.q: State true or false: (i) One must not accept one's age. (ii) Developing healthy attitudes does not help in coping with ageing.
questions.answer: (i) False. (ii) False.

questions.q: Name any two external changes of ageing.
questions.answer: Graying hair, ageing skin, wrinkles, shift in posture (any two).

questions.q: Name any two internal changes of ageing.
questions.answer: Changes in respiratory, gastrointestinal, cardiovascular and central nervous systems (any two).

questions.q: Name any two diseases of old age.
questions.answer: Dementia and Alzheimer's disease.

questions.q: Name two great achievers of late adulthood.
questions.answer: Mahatma Gandhi, Baba Amte, Ramakrishna Paramhansa, Mother Teresa (any two).

questions.q: Fill in: (i) Menopause occurs between ______ years. (ii) Erikson's crisis of middle age is ______ versus self-absorption.
questions.answer: (i) 45 and 50. (ii) generativity.

sections.title: Objective type questions: each has four parts of 1 mark.

questions.q: Give two characteristics each of (i) young adulthood; (ii) middle adulthood.
questions.answer: (i) Choice of career; starting a family. (ii) Competence, maturity; attention on children and plans for old age.

questions.q: Match the Erikson crisis: (i) young adulthood; (ii) middle adulthood; give (iii) the first term; (iv) the second term of the young adult crisis.
questions.answer: (i) Intimacy versus isolation. (ii) Generativity versus self-absorption. (iii) Intimacy. (iv) Isolation.

questions.q: Name any four elements of the key to a longer and healthier life.
questions.answer: Healthy diet, regular exercise, reduced stress, no smoking or alcohol (also positive qualities, social welfare, spirituality).

questions.q: Name any four coping strategies in old age.
questions.answer: Flexibility, trying new ways of coping, information seeking and problem solving, self-confidence and self-reliance.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: What is Grihastha Ashram?
questions.answer: The Indian stage of adulthood in which a person enters social life and accepts the responsibilities of family, marriage and career.

questions.q: What is intimacy versus isolation?
questions.answer: Erikson's crisis of young adulthood: forming deep intimate relationships, especially in marriage, or becoming socially and emotionally isolated.

questions.q: Why is middle age called a period of creativity?
questions.answer: The best works of scientists, writers and artists are produced in the late forties and early fifties.

questions.q: How does retirement affect people?
questions.answer: They lose jobs, readjust their lives, fear for their health and may feel insecure.

questions.q: Mention two cognitive changes with ageing.
questions.answer: Decline in memory and learning, reduced attention and speed of performance.

questions.q: How does a social network help the aged?
questions.answer: It allows sharing problems, emotional expression, approval, new experiences and trusting relationships.

questions.q: Why is the nuclear family a concern for cultural transmission?
questions.answer: Children lose elders who transmit culture through stories and morals, affecting their values and emotional expression.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Describe the characteristics of young adulthood.
questions.answer: Autonomy and independence, financial independence from parents, choice of career, starting a family, close peer relationships, concern for society; unemployment and marital discord are crises and intimacy versus isolation is the Erikson crisis.

questions.q: Describe the characteristics of middle adulthood.
questions.answer: Competence, maturity, responsibility and stability; attention on health, children and ageing parents and plans for old age; menopause in women; creativity; generativity versus self-absorption; turbulence from awareness of mortality.

questions.q: Explain the physical changes in ageing.
questions.answer: Organs decline by 0.8–1 per cent per year after 30; external changes are graying hair, wrinkles and posture changes; internal changes are in respiratory, digestive, cardiovascular and nervous systems; sensory abilities slow down.

questions.q: Explain the cognitive changes in ageing.
questions.answer: Memory, learning, attention and speed of performance decline, concentration and responsiveness decrease and dementia and Alzheimer's occur; older people also become more vulnerable.

questions.q: How can one cope with the problems of old age?
questions.answer: Accept one's age realistically and optimistically, be flexible, explore new coping methods, solve problems instead of withdrawing, build self-confidence, lead a disciplined life and use social support.

questions.q: Why are aged people important to society?
questions.answer: They hold knowledge, experience and wisdom, transmit culture to the young, and the joint family with elders supports multi-dimensional growth.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Describe young, middle and old adulthood.
questions.answer: Young adulthood (20s–30s): career, family, independence, intimacy versus isolation, age thirty transition. Middle adulthood (40s–50s): competence, stability, menopause, creativity, generativity versus self-absorption, turbulence and retirement planning. Old age (60+): retirement, health concerns, stereotypes, yet many remain active, with a store of wisdom.

questions.q: Discuss physical and cognitive changes during adulthood and old age and the key to healthy life.
questions.answer: Organs decline 0.8–1 per cent a year after 30; external changes (gray hair, wrinkles), internal changes (organ systems) and sensory slowing occur; memory, learning, attention and speed decline, with dementia and Alzheimer's. A healthy diet, exercise, less stress, no smoking or alcohol, social welfare and spirituality help.

questions.q: Explain how people can cope with the problems of old age and the role of social support.
questions.answer: Accept one's age, lead a disciplined life, be flexible, seek information and solve problems, build self-confidence and self-reliance. Social networks, clubs and friends give emotional expression and trust; grandparenting gives role-model status and satisfaction.

questions.q: Discuss the importance of the aged in society and the effect of breakdown of the family system.
questions.answer: Elders are repositories of knowledge and cultural transmission; the joint family supports growth in longevity, knowledge, fame and strength. The shift to nuclear families deprives children of stories and morals, affecting values and emotional expression and causing social problems.
